title: Stone Tools and Butchered Bones Push Back the Story of Chile's First Hunters
summary:
Archaeologists digging along the shore of an ancient lake in central Chile have found something remarkable: a large pile of bones from gomphotheres — extinct, elephant-like mammals — covered in cut marks and lying next to stone tools. The remains date to about 13,000 years ago, according to a September 24 statement from the Catalan Institute for Human Palaeoecology and Social Evolution (IPHES-CERCA).

Gomphotheres were tusked mammals related to modern elephants, and the bones turned up during two years of excavations in the Lake Tagua Tagua basin. The cut marks are the key clue. They suggest that Indigenous people butchered the animals at the site, not just scavenged them. The bones and artifacts date to roughly 12,000 to 13,000 years ago, which adds further evidence of early human occupation in southern South America.

This wasn't a one-time visit, either. Archaeologists had already found remains of now-extinct American horses and deer in the same basin, some with cut marks and signs of burning — evidence that ancient humans were cooking and eating them. Together, the finds suggest hunter-gatherers repeatedly returned to this lakeshore.

The earliest confirmed archaeological site in South America is Monte Verde, also in Chile, dated to about 14,500 years ago. Other early sites include Huaca Prieta in Peru and Arroyo Seco in Argentina, both around 14,000 years old.

IPHES-CERCA representatives called the assemblage "a record with no known parallels currently in South America." The site also preserved plant remains, giving researchers a fuller picture of how some of the first people to reach the Southern Cone lived and what they ate before the region's giant animals died out.

Now that fieldwork is complete, the team will analyze sediment and remains to narrow down exactly when humans first lived in the Lake Tagua Tagua basin — and how they killed, butchered, and ate the massive animals they encountered. Project co-director Carlos Tornero was among the researchers working in the excavation area.
why_it_matters: This discovery shows that human history is still being rewritten — evidence dug up today can overturn what textbooks said for decades — and it reminds us that the first Americans were not one group arriving at a single moment, but communities who settled, hunted and adapted across a whole continent.

background_read: For decades, many archaeologists believed the first Americans were the Clovis people, who left distinctive stone spear points across North America roughly 13,000 years ago.

The Monte Verde site in southern Chile (an ancient settlement dated to about 14,500 years ago) helped overturn that idea, because it showed people had already reached the far south of South America before Clovis tools appeared.

Most researchers now think the first people crossed from Siberia into North America across Beringia — a now-submerged land bridge between Russia and Alaska — during the last ice age, when sea levels were much lower.
Gomphotheres (extinct relatives of elephants with long, straight tusks) once roamed both the Americas, and like many large ice-age animals they died out around the end of the last ice age.
The Catalan Institute for Human Palaeoecology and Social Evolution, or IPHES-CERCA (a research centre based in Spain), announced the new finds at Lake Tagua Tagua in central Chile.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — hard evidence of early hunting
perspectives.description: Archaeologists see the cut-marked gomphothere bones as direct proof that people were actively butchering huge animals on this lakeshore, and the preserved plant remains add rare detail about what those first communities ate.

Cut marks prove that people used stone tools on a carcass, but some researchers argue they do not prove humans killed the animal, which may already have been dead. The dates also need independent confirmation before they can reshape the accepted timeline.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — part of a wider pattern
perspectives.description: The basin keeps producing the same kind of evidence: horses, deer and now gomphotheres, all with butchery marks. That fits a growing picture of mobile hunter-gatherer groups moving through southern South America as the ice age was ending.

Analyzing the sediment should pin down when people first used the basin and how the site was organised. Other ancient lakeshores in the region may hold similar sites that have not yet been excavated, potentially filling in the map of early settlement.
